source_title: Effects of a Dedicated Regional Psychiatric Emergency Service on Boarding of Psychiatric Patients in Area Emergency Departments
locator: Abstract; Methods and Results. Boarding measured from patient stable for psychiatric disposition to ED departure for transfer to the regional psychiatric emergency service (PES).
source_setting: Five community hospital EDs in Alameda County, California, operating under a regional psychiatric emergency service model for patients on involuntary mental-health holds.
source_n: 144 ED patients tracked across five hospitals.
quantity: Mean ED boarding time to transfer to regional PES
source_evidence_basis: Prospective operational tracking at five EDs. The full open-access original article defines the endpoint from psychiatric disposition stability to ED departure for PES transfer; reported mean was 107.56 minutes.
limitations: One county system and a 30-day cohort; regional PES availability and involuntary-hold workflow may not transfer to other settings. Mean is not a distribution, and comparison with older published benchmarks is not a controlled concurrent comparison. Not local RWJ data.
inferred_scenario_use: Model psychiatric disposition as assessment/stabilization followed by a dedicated PES transfer option. Use the measured mean only as an external point reference; do not infer a distribution or RWJ-specific wait.

source_title: Effects of a Dedicated Regional Psychiatric Emergency Service on Boarding of Psychiatric Patients in Area Emergency Departments
locator: Results; Table 2. Disposition after assessment and treatment in regional psychiatric emergency service.
source_setting: Same five Alameda County community EDs and regional PES; patients on involuntary mental-health holds.
source_n: 144 patients tracked at PES; article reports 37 admitted and 107 discharged.
quantity: Disposition after PES evaluation: inpatient psychiatric admission vs discharge
unit: percent of patients tracked at PES
source_evidence_basis: The full text explicitly reports 24.8% admitted and 75.2% discharged, and separately reports counts 37/144 and 107/144. These percentage and count statements conflict arithmetically: the reported counts imply 25.7% and 74.3%. The record preserves the published percentages and surfaces the discrepancy rather than silently recomputing them.
limitations: The article contains an internal percentage/count inconsistency: 37/144 and 107/144 do not equal its stated 24.8% and 75.2%. Resolve against author/source erratum before quantitative use. Single regional service and brief observation window; PES discharge does not establish outpatient follow-up or clinical outcome. Not RWJ data.
inferred_scenario_use: Represent assessment/treatment as a disposition branch between inpatient placement and PES discharge, but exclude the conflicting numeric percentages from calibration until the discrepancy is resolved; calibrate branch rates from local audited outcomes.

source_title: Predictors of Psychiatric Boarding in the Emergency Department
locator: Methods and Results; Table 1. Boarding defined as ED stay >4 hours after medical clearance among patients requiring inpatient psychiatric treatment.
source_setting: Retrospective cohort at two community EDs in Illinois; patients requiring inpatient psychiatric treatment and transfer to regional facilities.
source_n: 671 included encounters: private insurance n=120, Medicare/Medicaid n=312, self-pay/uninsured n=239.
unit: percent within insurance category boarding >4 hours after medical clearance
source_evidence_basis: Retrospective encounter cohort; table gives boarding counts of 94/120 privately insured, 224/312 Medicare/Medicaid, and 228/239 self-pay. Overall 546/671 boarded.
limitations: Two Illinois EDs, historical data and a study-specific >4-hour definition. Association is not causal; insurance category may proxy multiple placement constraints. Do not transfer these percentages as current or local rates.
inferred_scenario_use: Use as evidence that psychiatric placement access can vary with payer/funding pathway; represent payer authorization and destination availability as potential parallel blockers, then replace with local data.

source_title: Predictors of Psychiatric Boarding in the Emergency Department
locator: Results and Discussion. Mean ED length of stay compared by destination funding type among patients transferred for inpatient psychiatric care.
source_setting: Same two Illinois community EDs; patients transferred to public or private psychiatric facilities.
source_n: 671 total cohort; subgroup denominators for public vs private destination comparison were not reported in the cited Results passage.
quantity: Mean ED length of stay by receiving psychiatric facility funding type
source_evidence_basis: The paper reports mean ED stay of 1,661 minutes for patients transferred to publicly funded facilities versus 705 minutes for those transferred to private facilities (p<0.001). This endpoint is total ED length of stay, not a separately isolated placement-search interval.
limitations: Subgroup denominators unavailable in the cited passage; retrospective and limited to two EDs in 2010-2012. Total ED stay includes care before placement search and cannot be interpreted as placement wait alone.
inferred_scenario_use: Keep ED clinical evaluation and post-disposition placement search as separate states; treat destination funding type as a candidate context factor for scenario sensitivity, not a causal multiplier.

source_title: Acute Care Utilization After Recovery Coaching Linkage During Substance-Related Inpatient Admission: Results of Two Randomized Controlled Trials
locator: Abstract, Key Results; recovery-support engagement over six months after discharge.
source_setting: Inpatient adults with substance use disorder at Greenville Memorial Hospital, Greenville, South Carolina; two parallel single-center randomized trials.
source_period: Recruitment April 2018-June 2019 (study 1) and July 2019-March 2020 (study 2); six-month follow-up.
quantity: Engagement in recovery support services within six months post-discharge
unit: percent engaged in recovery support services
source_evidence_basis: Trial abstract reports higher self-reported recovery-support engagement for intervention vs control (84%, 95% CI 78-91; 34%, 95% CI 25-44; p<.001). Combined two-trial full text inspected.
limitations: Single-center pilot-trial setting; engagement outcome does not establish reduced overall acute-care use or clinical improvement. Not a psychiatric ED boarding endpoint and not RWJ data.
inferred_scenario_use: Represent inpatient addiction consultation/recovery-coach contact and post-discharge linkage as explicit transitions, with follow-up engagement measured separately from readmission or symptom outcomes. Do not assume this effect size locally.

source_title: Acute Psychiatric Hospital Licensing and Certification: Staffing Needs and Patient Observation (California Department of Public Health guidance)
locator: Official guidance, response on method for determining real-time psychiatric nursing staffing needs; admission assessments, shift acuity assessment, observation rounding.
source_setting: California acute psychiatric hospitals; state licensing and certification guidance describing hospital staffing practices and regulatory requirements.
source_n: Not applicable; official workflow guidance, not an outcome cohort.
quantity: Described patient assessment, acuity staffing, and observation workflow
value: Admission nursing assessment covers self-harm/aggression risk, medical concerns, strengths, needs and goals; physical and psychiatric evaluations and social-work/discharge-planning assessments also inform plans.
RN face-to-face acuity assessment several hours before shift end on each 8- or 12-hour shift; supervisor reviews acuity tool and staffing/skill-mix needs.
Mental-health workers primarily perform around-the-clock patient rounds at 5- or 15-minute intervals and report behavior changes to nursing staff.
Guidance describes structured therapeutic activities during waking hours and limited time alone/in rooms.
source_evidence_basis: Directly inspected California Department of Public Health page describes acute psychiatric hospital regulatory obligations and practices in answer to a staffing question.
limitations: California acute psychiatric hospital context; page summarizes regulatory and common practice details rather than a comparative study. It does not specify one staffing ratio, establish efficacy, or describe general ED staffing.
inferred_scenario_use: Model psychiatric observation as acuity-dependent work with recurring rounds, escalation to nursing staff, supervisor-reviewed staffing adjustments, and scheduled therapeutic activity; confirm local policy and staffing before operational use.
